extracted.intended_audience: public relations students and practitioners (program planners, researchers, communicators)
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for diagnosing public relations problems and conducting situation analyses and research to inform program objectives, stakeholder prioritization, strategy selection, and communication tactics.

rubrics_metrics.name: Value of systematic listening/research
rubrics_metrics.description: Prudence dictates the systematic listening to an organization’s publics through scientific research.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Systematic listening lets organizations 'close the loop' and reflect back how people react to corporate communications; without it organizations operate more like closed systems, leading to firefighting rather than prevention. Listening requires effort, skill, time, and money; the amount of information input determines openness of the system.

rubrics_metrics.name: Problem statement — present tense
rubrics_metrics.description: A useful problem statement summarizes what is known about the problem situation: It is written in the present tense, describing the current situation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid words such as 'will,' 'could,' and 'should' because they address desired future states rather than 'what’s happening now.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Problem statement — specificity and measurability
rubrics_metrics.description: Problem statements should describe the situation in specific and measurable terms.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Detail most or all of the following: What is the source of concern? Where is this a problem? When is it a problem? Who is involved or affected? How are they involved or affected? Why is this a concern to the organization and its publics? Include objective research and documentation (concrete measures).

rubrics_metrics.name: Problem statement — avoid implying solutions or blame
rubrics_metrics.description: A problem statement does not imply solutions or place blame.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If a statement implies a solution (e.g., 'We have a communication problem' or 'Poor training of the field staff is the problem'), strategies are predetermined and limited; instead define the problem so a range of strategies remain open.

rubrics_metrics.name: Situation analysis vs. problem statement
rubrics_metrics.description: A situation analysis is the unabridged collection of all that is known about the situation, its history, forces operating on it, and those involved or affected; a problem statement is a concise description.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use the situation analysis as the 'fact book' to expand and illustrate the problem statement. The analysis provides the background needed for program planning and objective setting.

rubrics_metrics.name: Include organization's mission, charter, bylaws, history, structure (Internal Factor)
rubrics_metrics.description: Statements of the organization’s mission, charter, bylaws, history, and structure should be part of the internal situation analysis.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These items give context for interpreting the problem and guide what is acceptable or feasible within the organization.

rubrics_metrics.name: Include lists/biographies/photos of key officers and managers (Internal Factor)
rubrics_metrics.description: Lists, biographies, and photos of key officers, board members, managers, and so forth are part of internal analysis.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Provides insight into leadership perspectives, spokesperson availability, and potential internal stakeholders.

rubrics_metrics.name: Describe programs, products, services, histories (Internal Factor)
rubrics_metrics.description: Descriptions and histories of programs, products, services, and so forth belong in internal analysis.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These descriptions help determine what aspects of the organization may be causing or affected by the problem.

rubrics_metrics.name: Include statistics about resources, budget, staffing, sales, profits, stockholders (Internal Factor)
rubrics_metrics.description: Statistics about resources, budget, staffing, sales, profits, stockholders, and so forth should be documented.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Quantitative data ground the situation analysis and aid in setting realistic objectives and assessing constraints.

rubrics_metrics.name: Document policy statements and procedures related to the problem (Internal Factor)
rubrics_metrics.description: Policy statements and procedures related to the problem situation must be included.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Understanding internal policies indicates what actions are permitted, required, or constrained.

rubrics_metrics.name: Collect position statements (quotations) by key executives (Internal Factor)
rubrics_metrics.description: Position statements (quotations) by key executives regarding the problem situation should be gathered.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Executive positions can shape public perception and internal responses; include them verbatim when possible.

rubrics_metrics.name: Describe how the organization currently handles the problem (Internal Factor)
rubrics_metrics.description: Description of how the organization currently handles the problem situation is required.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This shows past and current corrective actions, gaps, and potential sources of resistance or leverage.

rubrics_metrics.name: List internal stakeholders (Internal Factor)
rubrics_metrics.description: Descriptions and lists of the organization’s internal stakeholders should be prepared.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Internal stakeholders affect and are affected by program choices; identify roles and influence.

rubrics_metrics.name: List organizational two-way media for internal communication (Internal Factor)
rubrics_metrics.description: Lists of organizational media (two-way) for communicating with internal groups belong in the internal analysis.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate effectiveness of internal channels when planning internal aspects of the program.

rubrics_metrics.name: Collect media clippings and coverage about the organization (External Factor)
rubrics_metrics.description: Clippings from newspaper, magazine, trade publication, newsletter, and online coverage of the organization and the problem situation should be collected.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use media coverage to understand public framing, misinformation, and issue salience.

rubrics_metrics.name: Gather reports/transcripts/tapes of broadcast coverage (External Factor)
rubrics_metrics.description: Reports, transcripts, and tapes of radio, television, and cable coverage should be included.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Broadcast materials may reach different audiences and shape perceptions differently than print/online.

rubrics_metrics.name: Conduct content analyses of media and Internet sources (External Factor)
rubrics_metrics.description: Content analyses of media coverage and Internet sources—websites, blogs, social media, and so on—are part of the external analysis.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Systematic content analysis helps quantify themes, tones, and trends across outlets.

rubrics_metrics.name: Compile list of media contacts and influencers (External Factor)
rubrics_metrics.description: Lists of media, journalists, columnists, talk-show hosts, freelance writers, online bloggers, websites, and producers who report news and features about the organization and issues related to the problem situation should be prepared.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Knowing who covers the issue helps target outreach and anticipate coverage angles.

rubrics_metrics.name: Identify groups and individuals who support the organization (External Factor)
rubrics_metrics.description: Lists of and background information on individuals and groups who share the organization’s concerns, interests, and positions on the problem situation (including their controlled media outlets).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Map allies, their reach, and potential channels for amplification or coalition-building.

rubrics_metrics.name: Identify groups and individuals who oppose the organization (External Factor)
rubrics_metrics.description: Lists of and background information on individuals and groups who oppose the organization’s concerns, interests, and positions (including their controlled media outlets).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Understanding opponents clarifies threats, likely criticisms, and bargaining positions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Include survey and public opinion poll results related to the problem (External Factor)
rubrics_metrics.description: Results of surveys and public opinion polls related to the organization and the problem situation should be included.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use these to quantify public awareness, attitudes, and shifts over time—assess representativeness and methodology.

rubrics_metrics.name: Schedule of special events, observances, and important dates (External Factor)
rubrics_metrics.description: Schedules of special events, observances, and other important dates related to the organization and the problem situation belong in external analysis.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Timing of outreach or announcements should account for calendars, anniversaries, and competing events.

rubrics_metrics.name: List government agencies, legislators, and officials with power (External Factor)
rubrics_metrics.description: Lists of government agencies, legislators, and other officials with regulatory and legislative power affecting the organization and the problem situation are necessary.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Identify regulators and policymakers to manage compliance, advocacy, or stakeholder engagement.

rubrics_metrics.name: Collect copies of relevant regulations, legislation, bills, and reports (External Factor)
rubrics_metrics.description: Copies of relevant regulations, legislation, pending bills, referenda, government publications, and hearing reports should be gathered.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Legal and regulatory context can create constraints or opportunities for communication and action.

rubrics_metrics.name: Include published research on related topics (External Factor)
rubrics_metrics.description: Copies of published research on topics related to the problem situation belong in external analysis.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use academic and sector research to inform strategy and avoid repeating past mistakes.

rubrics_metrics.name: List important reference books, records, and directories (External Factor)
rubrics_metrics.description: Lists of important reference books, records, and directories, as well as their locations in the organization, should be maintained.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ensure easy access to factual materials for rapid response (e.g., journalists' queries).

rubrics_metrics.name: Communication audit
rubrics_metrics.description: A communication audit is a systematic documentation of an organization’s communication efforts for the purpose of understanding how it communicates with its publics.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Audits evaluate vehicles (newsletters, annual reports, websites, etc.) for accuracy, timeliness, usefulness, and may recommend revamping or discontinuing ineffective channels.

rubrics_metrics.name: Stakeholder analysis and prioritization
rubrics_metrics.description: Stakeholder analysis identifies who is involved and who is affected in a situation and ranks or rates them according to interdependence with the organization in a particular problem situation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prioritize publics based on which stakeholders are most central to the particular problem and program goal—not on past efforts or routine approaches. Not all stakeholders need be target publics.

rubrics_metrics.name: Answer four research questions about publics' information behavior
rubrics_metrics.description: Research must determine: (1) How much do people use information in the problem situation? (2) What kinds of information do people use or seek? (3) How do people use information? (4) What predicts information use?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Design research to reveal needs and uses—programs should respond to audience needs, not solely to source interests; 'why' questions are common but hardest to answer via communication.

rubrics_metrics.name: Set objectives only after complete situation analysis
rubrics_metrics.description: Only after the situation has been completely analyzed can practitioners set realistic program goals.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Incomplete analysis can lead to overpromises, underdelivery, and programs that don't address root causes; PR cannot fix bad performance or lack of integrity.

rubrics_metrics.name: SWOT/TOWS analysis and strategic implications
rubrics_metrics.description: Summarize situation analysis findings in a SWOT (strengths, weaknesses, opportunities, threats) or TOWS framework to derive strategy.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: SO strategies: build on strengths to exploit opportunities. ST strategies: build on strengths to counter threats. WO strategies: minimize weaknesses to take advantage of opportunities. WT strategies: minimize both weaknesses and threats.

rubrics_metrics.name: Force-field analysis
rubrics_metrics.description: Use force-field analysis to brainstorm negative forces causing the problem and positive forces alleviating it, then weigh their relative contributions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Research helps determine extent of each force; targeted strategic decisions then minimize negative forces and maximize positive forces.

rubrics_metrics.name: Research follows the scientific method
rubrics_metrics.description: Research begins with a clear statement of the problem, then develops a research design and selects methods for gathering, analyzing, and interpreting data.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Choose survey, experiment, existing records, or published sources based on the problem; practitioners must understand research concepts even when outsourcing to specialists.

rubrics_metrics.name: Choose methods based on problem, skills, resources, and constraints
rubrics_metrics.description: Approach and methods chosen depend on the problem, the researcher's skills and preferences, available resources, and constraints imposed by others or the situation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Informal and formal methods differ primarily in sample selection and size and thus in generalizability.

rubrics_metrics.name: Limitations of informal/exploratory methods
rubrics_metrics.description: Informal methods are useful for detecting and exploring problems but have samples of unknown representativeness.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Results may represent vocal minorities or volunteers, not the broader public; using informal methods as definitive descriptions or to generalize is misuse. Treat them as exploratory/pretesting tools.

rubrics_metrics.name: Personal contact and observation as research method
rubrics_metrics.description: Personal contact and direct observation help practitioners size up awareness, opinions, and attitudes firsthand.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: staff posing as patients, working in wheelchairs, visiting shareholders at home, mobile information centers at events. Useful for contextual understanding and early warning but not for statistical inference.

rubrics_metrics.name: Key informants (in-depth interviews)
rubrics_metrics.description: Talk with knowledgeable leaders and experts via open-ended interviews to gather in-depth perspectives.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Limited to small number due to time and analysis needs; selected informants may not reflect less-informed followers but can provide early-warning signals and expert insight.

rubrics_metrics.name: Focus groups — purpose and structure
rubrics_metrics.description: Focus groups are structured group discussions (typically 6 to 12 carefully selected representatives) to explore reactions and gather information for questionnaire development or pretesting.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Sessions are videotaped and analyzed; an effective moderator is critical. Use for exploratory insights and serendipitous findings; do not treat focus group results as representative of a larger population.

rubrics_metrics.name: Focus group limitations and moderator effects
rubrics_metrics.description: Limitations include small nonrandom samples, artificial group context, selection bias, and moderator influence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Analysts’ subjective filtering also affects interpretation. Focus groups should supplement, not replace, formal surveys.

rubrics_metrics.name: Online community panels as exploratory method
rubrics_metrics.description: Online community networks can create larger 'group' panels (hundreds to thousands) to respond to questions and try proposals.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Useful for ongoing feedback but questions about representativeness and artificial social-network effects keep this in the exploratory category.

rubrics_metrics.name: Community forums and public participation types
rubrics_metrics.description: Community forums (town halls, public hearings) solicit input; the nature of participation varies from pseudo-participation to full participation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Four types: (1) Pseudo-participation — meetings held for show with no intention to factor input. (2) Information-only — input attached but not necessarily used. (3) Consultation — seeking input that may affect final design. (4) Full participation — collaboration and shared decision-making. Genuine power sharing increases satisfaction; timing alone (early vs late) may not.

rubrics_metrics.name: Advisory committees and boards — use and pitfalls
rubrics_metrics.description: Advisory committees/boards can serve as continuous feedback mechanisms for long-running programs and detect opinion changes early.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Only appoint such bodies when genuinely prepared to consider and act on their advice; cosmetic use backfires because members detect tokenism.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ombudsman/ombuds officer role
rubrics_metrics.description: An ombuds officer listens to concerns of internal organizational publics and reviews organizational practices.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This role provides an internal feedback channel; ensure independence and responsiveness so employees trust and use the office.

rubrics_metrics.name: Test assumptions with audience research (example: Santa Barbara Zoo case)
rubrics_metrics.description: Always ask audiences rather than assume their opinions—informal research can reveal unexpected priorities that should reshape messaging.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use pretesting (even informal surveys) to avoid launching campaigns built on planners’ assumptions; example: condor campaign pivoted from recovery story to 'A Sense of Awe' after guest surveys.
